newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan may drop France's Mistral for U.S. missiles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan may drop France's Mistral for U.S. missiles.

text.p: Taiwan may drop a French deal and buy more U.S. Stinger missiles since France, under strong pressure from communist China, has stopped arming the island, military officers said on Wednesday
"If we cannot get the Mistral missiles, we might turn to the American system," said Wang Chih-li, deputy executive director of defence ministry's arms acquisition office.
"Possibly the army would buy more Stinger missiles from the United States," he added.

Taipei had prepared a budget to buy Mistrals from France, but it has been impossible to ship them to Taiwan because Paris has refused export permits, Wang told Reuters when asked to comment on newspaper reports that deal may be scrubbed.
Taiwan has not said how much the Mistral deal is worth, but local media have put the cost of the 2,000 missiles and shoulder launchers ordered in 1993 at T$10 billion (US$360 million).
Under pressure from Beijing, Paris agreed in 1994 to halt all new arms sales to Taiwan, though it will complete delivery of 60 Mirage 2000-5 fighters ordered in 1992.
Wang said the Stingers could be cheaper.
"If we turn to the U.S. missiles, there shouldn't be a problem for us to buy more Stingers," he said.

The U.S. Defence Department in 1996 approved sales to Taiwan of 1,299 Stingers, 74 guided missile launchers, 74 flight trainer Stinger missiles, 96 Humvee vehicles and 500 rounds of .50 calibre ammunition for an estimated US$420 million.
In 1992 the Pentagon approved the sale of 150 F-16 fighter jets to Taiwan in a deal worth $3.4 billion. In 1993 it agreed to sell 200 Patriot antimissile missiles for some $175 million.

The weapons sales by France and the United States angered China, which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949 and opposes such arms sales as interference in China's domestic affairs.
Washington maintains a right to arm Taiwan despite its "one China" policy of recognising only Beijing's communists.
Taiwan took delivery on Tuesday of the first two F-16s, and China on Wednesday issued another blast against the United States, saying the move had seriously harmed Sino-U.S. relations.
France's 1994 agreement to stop arming Taiwan defused a row in which China had downgraded its Paris ties and frozen French contractors out of China business to protest the Mirage sale.
Beijing vows to use force to prevent moves by Taiwan towards independence and away from its stated advocacy of eventual reunification with the mainland.
China rattled Taiwan with war games and missile tests in nearby waters between 1995 and 1996 in what it acknowledged was a bid to intimidate the island away from hopes of independence.
Taiwan's National Security Bureau chief said on Wednesday Taiwan and China were not likely to engage in a military confrontation in the next five years.
State radio quoted bureau director-general Yin Chung-wen as telling parliament that China was unlikely to launch military adventures in the Taiwan strait that divides them in the coming five years.
Yin nevertheless cautioned that with continued military build-ups in China and Nationalist-ruled Taiwan, it was difficult to predict what would happen after five years. He did not elaborate.
